notes:
I've put together notes for most of Isaiah 5, but some verses have little or nothing. I hit my search and page limits after two full commentary pages (Enduring Word and Precept Austin), and both cut off partway through. Everything else comes from search-result extracts. As you asked, I've left out what I couldn't find. The main gaps:
- **Verses 15–16, 21 and 23–24:** nothing verse-specific. **Verses 27–29:** only one older commentary, which just quotes the King James text with no comment.
- **Protestant differences:** none of the pages I read set the traditions against each other. What I found is under v. 4, and it's a difference of emphasis, not a stated debate.
- **No pages found** from bibleodyssey.org, netbible.org's own notes, catholic.com, oca.org, or about prosperity, word-of-faith or hyper-grace teaching on this chapter.

**v. 1**
- **The singer:** Ellicott says the prophet takes the role of a minstrel singing one of the love songs his hearers enjoyed, with echoes of the Song of Solomon. The prophet presents himself, as it were, in the character of a minstrel, ready to sing to his hearers one of the love-songs in which their culture delighted (Amos 6:5.) In its language and rhythm it reminds us of the Song of Solomon. https://biblehub.com/commentaries/isaiah/5-1.htm
- **The "very fertile hill":** In Hebrew it is "a horn, son of oil." Barnes explains that "horn" means the top or point of a hill, and the fertility shows God had good reason to expect growth. The word "horn" used here in the Hebrew, denotes the "brow, apex," or sharp point of a hill. https://biblehub.com/commentaries/isaiah/5-1.htm
- **Who is "my beloved":** Readings differ.
  - Matthew Henry: God the Father wrote the song in honour of Christ, his beloved Son. God the Father dictates it to the honour of Christ his well beloved Son, whom he has constituted Lord of the vineyard. https://www.studylight.org/commentary/isaiah/5-1.html
  - Jamieson-Fausset-Brown: the Beloved is the Second Person of the Trinity, as God of the Jews, not yet as the incarnate Messiah. "The Beloved" is Jehovah, the Second Person, the "Angel" of God the Father, not in His character as incarnate Messiah, but as God of the Jews https://biblehub.com/commentaries/isaiah/5-1.htm
  - Gill mentions a view that the "beloved" was Isaiah's uncle, King Amaziah, but takes it to mean God or Christ. https://biblehub.com/commentaries/isaiah/5-1.htm
- **Luther's "cousin":** Luther, following the Latin Vulgate, translated the word as "cousin." Keil & Delitzsch reject this. It was a song of his dearest one (not his cousin, as Luther renders it… ) touching his vineyard. https://www.preceptaustin.org/isaiah_5_commentary
- **The vineyard as a bride:** Constable reads "vineyard" as a picture of a bride. Isaiah painted a picture of a man cultivating his relationship with his wife, only to have her turn out to be disappointing. https://www.studylight.org/commentary/isaiah/5-1.html
- **Link to Jesus:** Ironside connects the song to Jesus' parable of the vineyard in Matthew 21:33. https://www.preceptaustin.org/isaiah_5_commentary
- **Catholic:** Haydock notes that the Hebrews had songs of sorrow as well as joy, and that the master of the vineyard is God himself. https://www.studylight.org/commentaries/eng/hcc/isaiah-5.html

**v. 2**
- **The owner's care:** Guzik lists everything the owner did: good soil, prepared ground, the best vines, a tower for protection, a winepress ready for the harvest. https://enduringword.com/bible-commentary/isaiah-5/
- **Sour or "wild" grapes:** Guzik says they are exactly what the vineyard would have produced if nothing had been done to it. https://enduringword.com/bible-commentary/isaiah-5/
- **Rotten fruit:** Jamieson-Fausset-Brown says the Hebrew word suggests putrid, offensive fruit, matching the people's corruption. https://www.studylight.org/commentaries/eng/jfu/isaiah-5.html The Catholic Encyclopedia agrees that "wild grapes" is too weak and suggests "stinking fruits." https://www.newadvent.org/cathen/12149a.htm
- **Reading each detail as a symbol:** Matthew Henry takes the details one by one: removing stones is God offering to take away the stony heart, the tower is the temple, the winepress is the altar. https://www.studylight.org/commentary/isaiah/5-1.html Jerome read the fence as angels, the stones as idols, the tower as the temple and the winepress as the altar. https://www.studylight.org/commentaries/eng/jfu/isaiah-5.html The Preacher's Homiletical Commentary pushes back. To seek thus for minute analogies is at once to destroy the oratorical force and the simplicity of the parable. https://www.studylight.org/commentaries/eng/phc/isaiah-5.html
- **Catholic:** Haydock says the "choicest vine" is *sorek* in Hebrew, and that angels guarded the vineyard. https://www.studylight.org/commentaries/eng/hcc/isaiah-5.html

**v. 3**
- **God speaks:** The Pulpit Commentary says the song ends here and God himself speaks. It compares Nathan's parable that trapped David (2 Samuel 12). https://studylight.org/commentaries/tpc/isaiah-5.html
- **Judging themselves:** The Cambridge Bible notes that, like Jesus' hearers in Matthew 21:41, the people agree to their own condemnation before they see the point. https://biblehub.com/commentaries/isaiah/5-1.htm

**v. 4**
- **The blame is not God's:** Guzik says God did everything he could short of turning people into robots. He also warns from 2 Corinthians 6:1 that God's grace can be received in vain. https://enduringword.com/bible-commentary/isaiah-5/
- **Grace and change:** Precept Austin quotes Ray Ortlund: God's grace both accepts and changes us, and "The power of grace is not automatic", so wanting acceptance without change wastes grace. https://www.preceptaustin.org/isaiah_5_commentary
- **Possible difference in emphasis:** The pages lean different ways, though none presents this as a debate between traditions.
  - Guzik quotes F.B. Meyer that "every soul of man had the chance of becoming a fruitful vineyard". https://enduringword.com/bible-commentary/isaiah-5/
  - An unnamed source quoted on Precept Austin stresses election instead: People deserved no credit for their election or their privileged status; it happened totally by grace. https://www.preceptaustin.org/isaiah_5_commentary

**vv. 5–6**
- **God withdraws:** Constable says the owner would stop protecting and caring for the vineyard, and even help destroy it. https://www.studylight.org/commentaries/eng/dcc/isaiah-5.html
- **Losing the "pruning":** Guzik says it is worse when God stops pruning and digging. He also links "taking away the hedge" to church discipline (1 Corinthians 5:4–5). https://enduringword.com/bible-commentary/isaiah-5/
- **The church's status:** Matthew Henry says the Jewish church would be "unchurched," fulfilled when Jerusalem was ploughed like a field (Micah 3:12). https://www.blueletterbible.org/Comm/mhc/Isa/Isa_005.cfm
- **Thorns:** The Catholic Encyclopedia identifies the Hebrew word for "thorns" (*shamir*) with a specific thorny plant (*Paliurus aculeatus*). https://www.newadvent.org/cathen/12149a.htm

**v. 7**
- **The wordplay:** Guzik explains the Hebrew pun: God looked for *mishpat* (justice) but found *mispach* (bloodshed), for *tsedaqah* (righteousness) but heard *tse'aqah* (a cry). https://enduringword.com/bible-commentary/isaiah-5/
- **What the pun suggests:** Constable quotes a writer who says the similar sounds show the bad grapes looked like good ones. In appearance at least the nation seemed to be the people of God. https://www.studylight.org/commentaries/eng/dcc/isaiah-5.html
- **"The plant of His delight":** Jamieson-Fausset-Brown links it to God's choosing of the Jews. https://www.studylight.org/commentaries/eng/jfu/isaiah-5.html

**vv. 8–10**
- **Greed, not owning land:** Guzik quotes Calvin that adding field to field is not wrong in itself. The target is a greed that is never satisfied. https://enduringword.com/bible-commentary/isaiah-5/
- **The poor harvest:** Matthew Henry explains that ten acres would give one bath (about eight gallons), and the harvest would be a tenth of the seed sown. https://www.blueletterbible.org/Comm/mhc/Isa/Isa_005.cfm
- **"Ten acres":** Jamieson-Fausset-Brown says it is literally ten "yokes," what one pair of oxen could plough in a day. https://www.studylight.org/commentaries/eng/jfu/isaiah-5.html

**vv. 11–12**
- **Forgetting God:** Guzik says the real problem with constant partying is that God is forgotten. https://enduringword.com/bible-commentary/isaiah-5/
- **"Strong drink":** Haydock says the Hebrew *shecar* means palm wine or any intoxicating drink. https://www.studylight.org/commentaries/eng/hcc/isaiah-5.html

**vv. 13–17**
- **Guzik's summary:** The coming captivity will end the laughter, lift up the Lord and reward the meek. https://enduringword.com/bible-commentary/isaiah-5/
- **Sheol (v. 14):** Barnes says Sheol here means the realm of the dead, without the idea of punishment. So many would die by famine and sword that it must "enlarge itself." https://www.studylight.org/bible/eng/esv/isaiah/5-14.html
- **The Geneva Bible notes:** the grave will swallow up them who will die for hunger and thirst, and yet for all this great destruction it will never be satisfied. https://biblehub.com/commentaries/isaiah/5-14.htm
- **Translation:** The NET Bible translates "Sheol" as "Death." https://biblehub.com/multi/isaiah/5-14.htm

**vv. 18–19**
- **"Cords of deceit":** Guzik says they pull sin toward themselves with empty ropes. He quotes Calvin that the "cords" are excuses that make sin seem smaller. https://enduringword.com/bible-commentary/isaiah-5/
- **Mocking God:** Guzik quotes Poole: their actions meant "let Him do his worst," though they would not have said it aloud. https://enduringword.com/bible-commentary/isaiah-5/

**v. 20**
- **Moral confusion:** Guzik calls it a deep state of moral confusion. https://enduringword.com/bible-commentary/isaiah-5/
- **Fair names for sins:** The Pulpit Commentary gives examples of dressing up sin, such as call cowardice caution, and rashness courage. https://biblehub.com/commentaries/isaiah/5-20.htm
- **Gill:** He also applies the verse to the scribes and Pharisees, who put their traditions above God's law. https://biblehub.com/commentaries/isaiah/5-20.htm
- **Catholic (Church Fathers):** Jerome uses the verse to argue that we must not praise our friends' faults. https://www.newadvent.org/fathers/3001084.htm
- **Translation:** The NET Bible says such people "are as good as dead." https://biblehub.com/parallel/isaiah/5-20.htm

**vv. 22–23**
- **Guzik:** He describes these as corrupt people who care more about drinking than about fairness and justice. https://enduringword.com/bible-commentary/isaiah-5/

**v. 25**
- **Constable** sees God taking away the hedge and breaking down the wall, as the song warned. https://www.studylight.org/commentaries/eng/dcc/isaiah-5.html

**v. 26**
- **Banner and whistle:** Ellicott says the banner marked where an army gathered, and the whistle was the sound signal. "The ends of the earth" points to the Assyrians. https://biblehub.com/commentaries/isaiah/5-26.htm
- **Bees:** Clarke cites Cyril of Alexandria: the picture is a beekeeper whistling his bees in and out. https://www.studylight.org/commentary/isaiah/5-26.html
- **Assyria:** Constable notes Assyria's army was proud of its speed. https://www.studylight.org/commentary/isaiah/5-26.html
- **Assyria and Babylon:** Bible.org sees both nations here. https://bible.org/article/isaiah-brief-commentary
- **Which enemy:** Precept Austin quotes Gary Smith: the enemy is left unnamed here, unlike Isaiah 7–8, where Assyria is named. https://www.preceptaustin.org/isaiah_5_commentary

**v. 30**
- **Applying it to the church:** Jamieson-Fausset-Brown applies the chapter to Christendom. A faithful remnant bears fruit, but the outward church as a whole is "found wanting." https://www.studylight.org/commentaries/eng/jfu/isaiah-5.html
